title: The Dutch Inside Your English
subtitle: The West Germanic twin, first articles, and your first Dutch sentences

summary.takeaway: Dutch is not a code to crack from scratch: the core vocabulary is a West Germanic warehouse, and the articles are the first key.

title: Hidden Twins: Body & Home
subtitle: arm, hand, vinger, hoofd, oog, oor — the body is the safest place to start

summary.takeaway: The body vocabulary is nearly free; the only new work is the article that travels with each noun.

title: The SCH Bridge
subtitle: English sh is Dutch sch — one sound, three letters

summary.takeaway: A spelling bridge is a free word: once you see sch, you can hear the English twin underneath.

title: SCH Spelling Gym
subtitle: shoe, sheep, shoulder, shadow — the sch block in the wild

summary.takeaway: Repetition is hidden by changing the word, not the pattern.

title: The TH → D Bridge
subtitle: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken

summary.takeaway: The rule is a hint for recognition, not a licence to predict every d word.

title: TH → D Discrimination
subtitle: brother, mother, father, thing — separate the twins from the lookalikes

summary.takeaway: A rule is strongest when you also know its exceptions.

title: The F → V & S → Z Bridges
subtitle: father → vader, fish → vis, sun → zon, sea → zee

summary.takeaway: Dutch spelling preserves a consonant history that the modern accent may hide.

title: Voicing Gym
subtitle: fish, fire, full, free, salt, seven — mixed f/v and s/z drills

summary.takeaway: Voicing is a family habit, not a list of exceptions.

title: The GH → CH Bridge
subtitle: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht

summary.takeaway: English spelling often preserves a sound English forgot; Dutch still says it.

title: CH & G Clinic
subtitle: nacht, licht, recht versus goed, groen, geven

summary.takeaway: Two sounds that English lumps together become a visible contrast in Dutch.

title: The Vowel Bridges
subtitle: ice → ijs, house → huis, book → boek — the real Dutch work

summary.takeaway: Vowels are where the course earns its keep; consonants are the free part.

title: IJ / UI / OE Gym
subtitle: ice, out, thousand, brown, mouse, book — three vowel families in one drill

summary.takeaway: One gliding vowel per digraph; do not split it into two English beats.

title: G, CH & Dutch Spelling
subtitle: yellow → geel, year → jaar, and the t that turns back into d

summary.takeaway: Dutch spelling is morphological: the word's family decides the letter.

title: Final Devoicing Gym
subtitle: hond/honden, huis/huizen, stad/steden — hear the change, keep the letter

summary.takeaway: Dutch spelling is a record of the word's family, not a phonetic transcript.

title: Zijn & Hebben
subtitle: to be, to have, and the Dutch way to say your age

summary.takeaway: Two verbs, two frames: being takes zijn, possession takes hebben, and age belongs to being.

title: Zijn & Have Gym
subtitle: ben/bent/is, heb/hebt/heeft — identity, possession and hunger

summary.takeaway: Dutch often says you 'have' a state English says you 'are'.

title: De & Het: Gender Without Case
subtitle: two articles, no noun case, and the compounds that decode them

summary.takeaway: Dutch gender is a two-way article system with no noun case — smaller than German, not random.

title: De/Het Decoder
subtitle: the last element of a compound decides the article

summary.takeaway: Compounds are a gender shortcut: read them from the end.

title: The Present Tense
subtitle: one stem, two endings, and the t that disappears in inversion

summary.takeaway: The stem is the launchpad; the endings follow the subject, and inversion changes the second-person shape.

title: Present Tense Drill
subtitle: werken, maken, leren, lezen, schrijven, spreken

summary.takeaway: Regular verbs are not memorised one by one; they are one stem plus three endings.

title: Niet & Geen
subtitle: niet for the sentence, geen for an indefinite noun

summary.takeaway: Negation is a decision about the noun phrase, not a single word you sprinkle on a sentence.

title: Niet/Geen Drill
subtitle: coffee, tea, time and water — choose the negator by what follows

summary.takeaway: The negator is chosen by the thing being negated, not by the speaker's mood.

title: Word Order: The Dutch Bracket
subtitle: the verb takes second place — front something else and it steps around the subject

summary.takeaway: Dutch word order is a position rule: the verb claims second place, and the subject moves around it.

title: Inversion Gym
subtitle: vandaag, morgen, hier, daar — front it and invert it

summary.takeaway: Inversion is the normal consequence of V2, not an emergency manoeuvre.

title: Modals & the Final Infinitive
subtitle: kan, moet, mag, wil, zal — the second verb waits at the end

summary.takeaway: The modal bracket is the same two-position idea as V2, stretched across two verbs.

title: Modal Gym
subtitle: kan, moet, mag, wil, zal — five modals, one shape

summary.takeaway: A modal is a slot, not a new sentence pattern.

title: Separable Verbs
subtitle: opbellen, meebrengen, aankomen — the prefix walks to the end

summary.takeaway: A separable verb is a bracket: one meaning, two halves, the rest of the sentence inside.

title: Separable Verb Gym
subtitle: opbellen, meebrengen, aankomen, uitwaaien, overstappen, pinnen

summary.takeaway: The prefix is a position, not a decoration; the sentence tells you where it goes.

title: Numbers & Time
subtitle: een, twee, drie — and why half drie means half past two

summary.takeaway: Dutch time is not a translation of English time; it is the same clock read from the other side.

title: Clock & Numbers Gym
subtitle: tien, twintig, honderd, duizend — and the half-hour trap

summary.takeaway: The clock is a rule, not a list: learn the anchor and the rest follows.

title: Days, Months & Dates
subtitle: maandag, januari, vandaag — the calendar words English and Dutch share

summary.takeaway: Calendar vocabulary is a loan; calendar grammar is a preposition choice.

title: Calendar Gym
subtitle: Monday to Saturday, and the days that take op

summary.takeaway: Day names are vocabulary; the time phrase is the grammar.

title: The Weak Past
subtitle: werk → werkte, maak → maakte — a small ending, not a new word

summary.takeaway: The past tense is a suffix on the stem, not a new vocabulary item.

title: Weak Past Gym
subtitle: werken, maken, spelen, leren, wonen, betalen — one ending at a time

summary.takeaway: Weak pasts are mechanical once you hear the stem.

title: The Strong Past
subtitle: kom → kwam, zie → zag, geef → gaf — the old vowel dance

summary.takeaway: Some pasts are vowel changes, not suffixes; English and Dutch share the habit.

title: Strong Verb Gym
subtitle: kwam, zag, gaf, nam — the core strong pasts in context

summary.takeaway: Strong verbs are a vowel system, not a list of exceptions.

title: The Perfect Tense
subtitle: ik heb gewerkt, ik ben gekomen — hebben or zijn plus the ge- participle

summary.takeaway: The perfect is a helper plus a participle; the helper is chosen by the verb's meaning.

title: Perfect Tense Gym
subtitle: gewerkt, gemaakt, gekomen, gegaan — build the participle and choose the helper

summary.takeaway: The perfect is a bracket: helper second, participle last.

title: The Future & the Would-World
subtitle: gaan + infinitive for plans; zou for the polite conditional

use_example.english: He is going to make it.

summary.takeaway: Dutch future is a choice of stance: going to, will, or would.

title: Future & Would Gym
subtitle: ik ga werken, wij zullen komen, ik zou kunnen gaan

summary.takeaway: Every future is still a bracket; the stance changes, the order does not.

title: Comparatives & Superlatives
subtitle: groot → groter → grootst; goed → beter → best

summary.takeaway: Comparison is one ending plus two tiny words: dan for than, als for as.

title: Comparison Gym
subtitle: groter, kleiner, sneller, langzamer — compare without translating 'than'

summary.takeaway: Comparison is a frame for two items; the adjective carries the degree.

title: Pronouns & Possessives
subtitle: mij, jou, hem, haar — the object set with a polite u

summary.takeaway: Nouns lost case; pronouns kept it. Dutch and English share that division.

title: Pronoun Gym
subtitle: mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons — possessives agree with the thing owned

summary.takeaway: Possessives track the owned noun, not the owner.

title: Reflexives & Daily Routine
subtitle: ik was me, ik voel me — Dutch uses a reflexive where English often uses nothing

summary.takeaway: A reflexive verb points the action back at its subject.

title: Reflexive Gym
subtitle: opstaan, aankleden, wassen, voelen — a day told through reflexives

summary.takeaway: Reflexive and separable patterns stack: first the pronoun, then the finite verb, then the prefix.

title: Er: The Little Word That Does Everything
subtitle: er is, er zijn, ik heb er twee — existence, place and 'of it'

summary.takeaway: Er is the grammatical 'there' — a small word with several structural jobs.

title: Er Gym
subtitle: er is, er zijn, er van, er mee — the four jobs of er in one drill

summary.takeaway: Er is a structural pronoun: it points to existence, place or quantity without naming it.

title: Subordinate Clauses
subtitle: omdat, dat, als — the verb leaves second place and waits at the end

summary.takeaway: The conjunction is the signal: subordinate clause, verb final.

title: Verb-Final Gym
subtitle: omdat, dat, als, wanneer, maar, hoewel

use_example.german: Ik werk, maar ik ben moe.
use_example.english: I work, but I am tired.

summary.takeaway: Connectors come in two species: those that move the verb and those that do not.

title: Relative Clauses & Connectors
subtitle: die, dat, wie, wat — choosing the relative pronoun by the noun

summary.takeaway: The noun's article decides the relative pronoun; the clause keeps subordinate order.

title: Relative Clause Gym
subtitle: de man die komt, het boek dat ik lees — choose die or dat

summary.takeaway: Relative pronouns point back; question words point forward. Both keep the verb in its clause's slot.

title: The Continuous & Position Verbs
subtitle: aan het werken, zitten te lezen — Dutch builds 'is doing' with a posture verb

summary.takeaway: Dutch 'is doing' is a picture: on the doing, or sitting/standing/lying to do.

title: Continuous Gym
subtitle: ik ben aan het werken, zij zit te lezen, hij staat te wachten

summary.takeaway: The continuous is a picture plus an infinitive; the posture is optional colour.

title: Dutch Idioms & Directness
subtitle: lekker, gezellig, doe normaal, graag — the words that make Dutch sound Dutch

summary.takeaway: Dutch often expresses desire and pleasure with small possessed nouns and adverbs, not with 'like'.

title: Idiom Gym
subtitle: zin in thee, trek in vis, lekker eten, gezellig — desire and comfort

summary.takeaway: Idioms are small grammatical habitats, not vocabulary decorations.

title: Diminutives & Word Formation
subtitle: -je, -tje, -pje, -etje — the diminutive is Dutch's favourite word-building machine

summary.takeaway: The diminutive is a word-building machine that also resets the article to het.

title: Diminutive Gym
subtitle: broodje, kopje, huisje, appeltje, bloemetje, hondje

summary.takeaway: The diminutive ending is predictable from the noun's final sound; the article is always het.

summary.takeaway: Dutch profession phrases are a small article rule, not a vocabulary list.
